There isn't a single "best" app—it depends entirely on **what you prioritize** (privacy, features, who you’re talking to, or ecosystem). Here is a breakdown by category to help you decide:

---

### 🥇 **Best for Privacy & Security (Gold Standard)**
| App | Best For | Key Trade-offs |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Signal** | **Maximum privacy.** Open source, end-to-end encryption (E2EE) by default for everything (chats, calls, video), minimal metadata collection, non-profit funded. | Smaller user base (you have to convince friends to switch); no cloud backup for message history (local only); fewer "fun" features (stickers, stories). |
| **Session** | **Anonymity.** No phone number/email required (uses decentralized routing). | Very niche; slower message delivery; limited features. |
| **Threema** | **Privacy without a phone number.** Paid app (one-time fee), Swiss-based, ID-based (not phone number). | Costs ~$4–$5; smaller user base; mostly popular in Europe. |

---

### 🌍 **Best for "Everyone Is Already On It" (Network Effect)**
| App | Best For | Key Trade-offs |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **WhatsApp** | **Global reach.** Billions of users; E2EE by default; great voice/video calls; works on slow connections. | Owned by Meta (data sharing concerns for advertising); requires phone number; backups to Google Drive/iCloud are *not* E2EE by default (must enable manually). |
| **iMessage** | **Apple ecosystem.** Seamless SMS/E2EE hybrid; high-quality media sharing; no extra app needed if you have an iPhone. | **Apple only** (green bubbles for Android); locked into ecosystem; iCloud backups not E2EE by default (enable "Advanced Data Protection"). |
| **Google Messages (RCS)** | **Android default.** Replacing SMS; E2EE in 1-on-1 chats; high-res media; works via web browser. | E2EE not in group chats yet; carrier/Google dependence; fragmented support on iPhone (Apple adopting RCS late 2024). |
| **Telegram** | **Features & Communities.** Massive groups (200k+), channels, bots, huge file sharing (2GB), cloud sync across devices. | **Not E2EE by default** (only in "Secret Chats"); cloud chats stored on their servers; metadata collection; often used for piracy/scams. |

---

### 💼 **Best for Work / Productivity / Communities**
| App | Best For | Key Trade-offs |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Slack** | **Workplace collaboration.** Threads, integrations (GitHub, Jira, Google Drive), huddles, searchable history. | Expensive for large history; not for personal use; no E2EE. |
| **Discord** | **Communities/Gaming/Study groups.** Voice channels, persistent servers, bots, streaming, free. | Not E2EE; data mining for ads; can be overwhelming/cluttered UI. |
| **Microsoft Teams** | **Enterprise/Microsoft 365 shops.** Deep Office integration, video meetings, file collaboration. | Heavy resource usage; clunky for personal use. |
| **Matrix (Element)** | **Decentralized/Federated.** Open protocol; you own your data; bridges to Slack/Discord/IRC; E2EE. | Steeper learning curve; server setup/maintenance (unless using matrix.org); client apps vary in polish. |

---

### 🎨 **Best for Features & Customization (Power Users)**
*   **Telegram:** Best cloud sync, massive files, bots, themes, "Saved Messages" (cloud clipboard).
*   **Discord:** Best for persistent community servers with voice/video/text mix.

---

### 🛡️ **Best for Specific Threat Models**
*   **Journalists/Activists in high-risk zones:** **Signal** (disappearing messages, sealed sender, registration lock) or **Briar** (offline/Bluetooth mesh, no internet needed).
*   **Avoiding Phone Numbers:** **Signal** (now supports usernames), **Session**, **Threema**, **Wire**, **Matrix/Element**.
*   **Self-Hosting / Total Data Control:** **Matrix (Synapse/Dendrite server + Element client)**, **XMPP (Conversations app)**, **Rocket.Chat**, **Mattermost**.

---

### 🧭 **Quick Decision Guide: "Pick *One* For Me"**

| **If your situation is...** | **Start with...** |
| :--- | :--- |
| **"I just want the most private option, period."** | **Signal** |
| **"I need to talk to Grandma/uncle in another country *right now*."** | **WhatsApp** (or **iMessage** if all Apple) |
| **"I run a community/club/gaming group."** | **Discord** |
| **"I need this for my job/team."** | **Slack** (or **Teams** if corporate M365) |
| **"I hate giving out my phone number."** | **Signal (usernames)** or **Session** / **Threema** |
| **"I want Telegram features but better privacy."** | **No perfect clone exists.** Matrix/Element is closest architecturally, but UX differs. |
| **"I use Android and want the best SMS upgrade."** | **Google Messages (RCS)** |

---

### ⚠️ **Critical Tip: The "Backup" Loophole**
Even if you use **Signal** or **WhatsApp** (E2EE), **your backups might not be encrypted.**
*   **Signal:** Backups are local/encrypted passphrase only. No cloud backup (by design).
*   **WhatsApp:** **Turn on "End-to-End Encrypted Backup"** in Settings > Chats > Chat Backup. Otherwise, Google Drive/iCloud backups are readable by Apple/Google/governments.
*   **iMessage:** Enable **Advanced Data Protection** in iCloud settings to encrypt backups.

---

### 💡 **My Practical Advice**
**Install 2 apps:**
1.  **Signal** (for your inner circle, family, sensitive chats).
2.  **WhatsApp / iMessage / Google Messages** (for the "rest of the world" who won't switch).

This gives you privacy where it matters and compatibility everywhere else.

runs.u: Which one would you pick?
runs.reply:
**I can’t pick one for *myself* because I don’t have a phone, friends, or a threat model.** I don’t face the trade-offs you do (battery life, convincing Grandma to install an app, government surveillance, or needing to share 4K videos).

**But if I were *you*, I’d pick based on which of these 3 profiles fits your life right now:**

---

### 🎯 **Profile A: "I want the best privacy *without* becoming a hermit."**
> **My Pick: Signal (Primary) + WhatsApp/iMessage (Secondary for everyone else).**

*   **Why:** You get gold-standard encryption for your inner circle (partner, parents, close friends, work secrets). For the other 90% of contacts who refuse to switch, you keep the mainstream app installed but treat it as "public broadcast."
*   **The Workflow:**
    *   *Signal:* "Leaving now," medical stuff, passwords, finances, private vents.
    *   *WhatsApp/iMessage:* Group chats for the soccer team, memes from college friends, the plumber, delivery drivers.

---

### 🎯 **Profile B: "I run communities / I hate switching apps / I want features."**
> **My Pick: Discord (Communities) + Google Messages / iMessage (Personal SMS fallback).**

*   **Why:** You need threads, voice channels, bots, 200-person servers, and searchable history. Signal/WhatsApp are terrible for *communities* (clunky groups, no threads, history limits).
*   **The Trade-off:** You accept zero E2EE on Discord. You treat it like a public forum. For actual private 1-on-1s, you fall back to Signal or your phone’s default RCS/iMessage.

---

### 🎯 **Profile C: "I am high-risk / I refuse phone numbers / I want total control."**
> **My Pick: Matrix (Element client) + Session / SimpleX.**

*   **Why:** You don't trust central servers (Meta, Google, Signal Foundation). You want to own your data, use a username (not a phone number), and potentially host your own server.
*   **The Reality Check:** This is **high friction**. You will be the only person in your contacts using it. You will troubleshoot federation errors. Pick this only if *ideology > convenience*.

---

### 🤖 **If you force me to simulate a "Daily Driver" choice:**

**I would run Signal as my default SMS/app hybrid (where Android allows) or primary chat app.**

**Reasoning:**
1.  **Architecture:** The Signal Protocol is the cryptographic backbone of WhatsApp, Google Messages (RCS), Facebook Messenger (Secret Conv), and Skype. Using Signal means using the *source*, not a fork.
2.  **Incentives:** It’s a 501(c)(3) non-profit. No ads, no VC pressure to monetize my social graph, no AI training on my messages.
3.  **Features caught up:** Usernames (no phone number sharing), stories, reactions, stickers, chat folders, link previews—it’s no longer "bare bones."
4.  **Discipline:** It forces *me* to be intentional. If a chat matters, I move it to Signal. If they won't install it, the chat probably didn't need E2EE anyway.

---

### **The "Cheat Code" Answer**
**Don't pick one. Pick a *stack*.**
> **Signal (Privacy) + WhatsApp/iMessage (Reach) + Discord/Slack (Work/Communities).**

It takes 5 minutes to install all three. You stop optimizing the *tool* and start optimizing the *conversation*.

runs.u: Can you recommend a ride-hailing app?
runs.reply:
The "best" ride-hailing app depends entirely on **where you are located** (or traveling to), as the market is highly fragmented by region. There is no single global winner.

Here is a breakdown by region and use case to help you choose:

---

### 🌍 **By Region (The Most Critical Factor)**

#### **United States & Canada**
*   **Uber:** Largest coverage, most vehicle options (UberX, Comfort, Black, Green, Pet, WAV), best airport integration.
*   **Lyft:** Strong #2 competitor. Often slightly cheaper or better driver treatment reputation. Good "Lyft Pink" subscription for frequent riders.
*   **Wingz / Alto:** Good for **scheduled/airport rides** with flat rates and employed drivers (Alto).

#### **Europe**
*   **Uber:** Works in major capitals (London, Paris, Berlin, Madrid, Amsterdam), but often limited to **Black/Lux/Van** (professional drivers only) due to regulations. UberX (peer-to-peer) is banned in many countries.
*   **Bolt (formerly Taxify):** **The main Uber alternative in Eastern/Central Europe & Africa.** Often cheaper than Uber; huge in Tallinn, Prague, Warsaw, Lisbon, London.
*   **Free Now (formerly MyTaxi):** **Dominant in Germany, Austria, Spain, Ireland, UK.** Aggregates licensed **taxis** + private hire. Great if you prefer regulated cabs.
*   **Cabify:** Strong in **Spain, Portugal, Latam**. Focus on premium service/corporate accounts.
*   **Heetch:** Popular in **France, Belgium, Italy, Morocco, Algeria**. "Social" vibe, often cheaper night rides.
*   **Yandex Go:** **Russia, Belarus, Kazakhstan, Armenia** (formerly Yandex Taxi).

#### **Latin America**
*   **Uber:** Dominant in **Mexico, Brazil, Colombia, Chile, Argentina, Peru, Costa Rica, Panama, DR, Ecuador, Uruguay**.
*   **DiDi:** Huge in **Mexico, Brazil, Colombia, Chile, Argentina, Panama, Costa Rica, Peru**. Often aggressively priced (cheaper than Uber).
*   **Cabify:** Strong in **Argentina, Chile, Colombia, Peru, Ecuador, Mexico, Panama, Peru, Uruguay**. Premium focus.
*   **Beat:** Was big in Greece/Latam; **acquired by DiDi/Free Now in most markets** (check local status).
*   **99 (99Pop):** **Brazil only.** Massive market share (owned by DiDi).
*   **InDrive:** **Rapidly growing in Latam (Mexico, Colombia, Peru, etc.).** Unique **"Negotiate your fare"** model (passenger sets price, driver accepts/counters).

#### **Asia Pacific**
*   **Grab:** **The "Super App" of Southeast Asia.** Dominant in **Singapore, Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand, Vietnam, Philippines, Cambodia, Myanmar**. Offers food, packages, payments, financial services.
*   **Gojek:** **Indonesia's champion** (merged with Tokopedia -> GoTo). Massive in Indonesia; operates in Singapore, Vietnam, Thailand.
*   **DiDi (DiDi Chuxing):** **China (Mainland).** The absolute king. International version exists but Chinese version requires Chinese phone number/WeChat/Alipay.
*   **Gaode (Amap) / Baidu Maps:** **China.** Aggregators. You book via map apps; they dispatch DiDi, CaoCao, T3, etc. Best for visitors.
*   **Ola / Uber / Rapido / Namma Yatri:** **India.** Ola (auto/taxi/bike), Uber (premium/cabs), Rapido/Namma Yatri (bike/auto - zero commission).
*   **Kakao T / UT / Tada:** **South Korea.** Kakao T is the default (taxi-hailing). Tada = premium van/taxi.
*   **GO / JapanTaxi / DiDi / Uber:** **Japan.** **GO** is the current market leader (merger of JapanTaxi/MOV). Uber exists but is mostly **Black/Taxi** in Tokyo/Osaka. DiDi partners with local taxi cos.
*   **Bolt:** Growing in **Taiwan, Pakistan, Australia, New Zealand**.
*   **Ola / Uber / DiDi (exited ANZ) / Bolt:** **Australia & New Zealand.** Ola & Uber are duopoly. Bolt is new challenger.

#### **Middle East & Africa**
*   **Careem (owned by Uber):** **UAE, Saudi Arabia, Jordan, Pakistan, Egypt, Morocco, Qatar, Bahrain, Kuwait, Lebanon, Iraq.** The regional giant.
*   **Uber:** Works alongside Careem in Gulf/MENA (often same backend now).
*   **Bolt:** **South Africa, Nigeria, Kenya, Ghana, Egypt, Tunisia, Pakistan.** Very strong challenger.
*   **inDrive:** **Very popular in Nigeria, Egypt, South Africa, Kazakhstan, Latam.** Fare negotiation model.
*   **Yassir:** **Algeria, Tunisia, Morocco, France.** "Super App" model (rides, delivery, payments).
*   **Max.ng / Gokada:** **Nigeria (Lagos).** Started as bike-hailing (okada), pivoted to cars/logistics.

---

### 🎯 **By Specific Need / Feature**

| Need | Best App(s) | Why? |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Cheapest Price** | **inDrive** (negotiate fare), **Bolt**, **DiDi**, **Local Taxi Apps** | inDrive lets you set the price; Bolt/DiDi often subsidize heavily. |
| **Premium / Business / Luxury** | **Uber Black / Comfort**, **Free Now (Business)**, **Cabify**, **Blacklane**, **Wheely** | Guaranteed high-end cars, pro drivers, quiet mode, expense reporting. |
| **Scheduled / Airport (Fixed Price)** | **Wingz**, **Alto**, **Blacklane**, **Local Airport Taxi Apps** | No surge pricing; guaranteed pickup; meet & greet options. |
| **Safety Features (Women/ LGBTQ+)** | **Shebah** (Aus - women only), **Safr** (US - women focused), **Uber/Lyft/Bolt** (Share Trip, PIN verification, Audio Recording) | Major apps have improved: "Share Trip," "RideCheck," 911 integration, women-only driver options (where legal). |
| **Motorcycle / Tuk-Tuk / Auto-Rickshaw** | **Grab / Gojek / GoJek** (SE Asia), **Rapido / Namma Yatri / Ola Auto** (India), **Gokada / Max** (Nigeria), **inDrive / Bolt** (select cities) | Essential for beating traffic in dense megacities. |
| **Accessibility (Wheelchair / Assistance)** | **Uber WAV / Assist**, **Lyft Access**, **Free Now (Wheelchair)**, **Local Paratransit / Dial-a-Ride** | Uber/Lyft have dedicated WAV fleets in major cities; taxis often legally required to have % accessible. |
| **No Smartphone / For Seniors** | **GoGoGrandparent** (US/Can), **Arrive Rides** (US), **Local Taxi Phone Numbers** | Call a landline; they book Uber/Lyft for you & text updates to family. |
| **Eco-Friendly (EV / Hybrid Only)** | **Uber Green / Comfort Electric**, **Lyft Green Mode**, **Bolt Green**, **Free Now Electric**, **Local EV-only fleets (e.g., Revel - NYC)** | Filters for zero/low emission vehicles. |

---

### 💡 **Pro Tips for Choosing & Using**

1.  **Install 2-3 Apps:** Prices vary wildly minute-to-minute (surge pricing). Compare **Uber vs. Bolt vs. Lyft vs. Free Now vs. inDrive** before booking. Screenshotting quotes helps.
2.  **Check "Hidden" Fees:** Some apps charge **booking fees, service fees, airport surcharges, wait time fees, cross-border fees** (e.g., UberX Saver vs Priority).
3.  **Airport Rules:** Many airports have **designated pickup zones** (often parking garages/lots, *not* curb) and **authorized apps only**. Check the airport website *before* you land.
4.  **Local Taxi Apps:** Don't ignore them! **Free Now, Curb, Arro, Flywheel, local radio taxi apps** often have **fixed regulated fares, bus lane access, no surge, and professional drivers.** They can be faster/cheaper during surge.
5.  **Traveling Internationally?**
    *   Set up apps **before you leave** (verify phone number via SMS *at home*).
    *   Add **international payment method** (Revolut, Wise, credit card no FX fees).
    *   Download **offline maps** of the city.
    *   Learn **key phrases** ("Driver, I am at [Landmark], wearing [Color]").
6.  **inDrive Strategy:** If using inDrive (negotiation), **start 10-15% below estimated fare**. Drivers counter. Good for non-urgent rides.
7.  **Subscriptions:** If you ride >3-4x/week, **Uber One / Lyft Pink / Bolt+ / GrabUnlimited** often pay for themselves via $0 delivery fees, priority support, ride discounts.

---

### 🤔 **Still unsure? Tell me:**
1.  **City/Country** you need the ride in.
2.  **Typical trip type** (Daily commute? Airport? Night out? Intercity? With kids/pets/luggage? Wheelchair?).
3.  **Priority** (Absolute cheapest? Fastest pickup? Nicest car? Safety? Cash payment?).
4.  **Do you have a local SIM/phone number?** (Critical for Asia/China/Latam apps).

With that info, I can give you the **single best recommendation + backup**.

To give you the best recommendation, **please tell me which city and country you are in (or traveling to).**

In the meantime, here is a breakdown of the major players by region:

---

### 1. Globally Dominant / Western Markets
*   **Uber:** Available in ~70+ countries. Best coverage in US, Canada, UK, Australia, Western Europe, Latin America.
*   **Lyft:** **US & Canada only.** Often cheaper than Uber in the US; good for scheduled rides.
*   **Bolt (formerly Taxify):** Strong in **Eastern Europe, Africa, UK, Scandinavia, Latin America**. Often cheaper than Uber.
*   **Free Now (formerly MyTaxi):** **Western/Central Europe** (Germany, France, Spain, Ireland, UK, Austria, Portugal). Focuses on licensed taxis + private hire.

---

### 2. Asia-Pacific Giants
*   **Grab:** **Southeast Asia** (Singapore, Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand, Vietnam, Philippines, Cambodia, Myanmar). *Super-app: food, groceries, payments.*
*   **Gojek:** **Indonesia** (dominant), also Vietnam, Singapore, Thailand. *Super-app: rides, food, logistics, payments.*
*   **DiDi (DiDi Chuxing):** **China** (dominant), also Australia, Japan, Mexico, Brazil, Chile, Colombia, Panama, Peru, Costa Rica, Taiwan, Hong Kong.
*   **Kakao T:** **South Korea** (Dominant). Integrates taxis, black cars, and transit.
*   **JapanTaxi / GO / Uber Taxi:** **Japan** (Uber operates mostly as a taxi-hailing partner here).
*   **inDrive:** **Global emerging markets** (LatAm, Africa, CIS, SEA, South Asia). **Unique feature:** You **negotiate the fare directly with the driver** (peer-to-peer pricing).
*   **BluSmart:** **India (Delhi/NCR, Bangalore)**. All-electric fleet, no surge pricing, no cancellations.
*   **Ola / Uber / Rapido:** **India** (Ola & Uber for cars/autos; Rapido for bike taxis).

---

### 3. Middle East & Africa
*   **Careem (owned by Uber):** **Middle East, Pakistan, Morocco, Jordan.** Very reliable; offers "Captain" (driver) loyalty perks.
*   **Bolt:** Strong in **South Africa, Nigeria, Kenya, Ghana, Tunisia, Pakistan.**
*   **Yassir:** **North/West Africa** (Algeria, Morocco, Tunisia, France, Canada, Germany).
*   **inDrive:** Very popular in **Nigeria, Egypt, South Africa, Kenya** due to fare negotiation.

---

### 4. Latin America
*   **Uber:** Dominant in major cities (Mexico City, São Paulo, Bogotá, Buenos Aires, Santiago, Lima).
*   **DiDi:** Huge competitor to Uber in **Mexico, Brazil, Chile, Colombia, Panama, Peru, Costa Rica.** Often cheaper.
*   **Beat (now part of Free Now/DiDi ecosystem):** Was big in **Greece, Peru, Chile, Colombia, Mexico** (check current status per city).
*   **Cabify:** **Spain, Portugal, Chile, Colombia, Peru, Mexico, Argentina, Uruguay, Ecuador.** Focus on premium/corporate service.
*   **99 (owned by DiDi):** **Brazil** (dominant alongside Uber).
*   **inDrive:** Growing rapidly across the region.

---

### 5. Specialty / Niche Apps
*   **Wingz:** **US Airports** (Flat-rate, pre-scheduled, no surge).
*   **Curb / Arro:** **US Cities** (Hail actual licensed **Yellow/Green Taxis** via app; pay via app).
*   **Blacklane / Wheely:** **Global Premium/Chauffeur** (Business class, fixed price, professional drivers).
*   **BlaBlaCar:** **Europe, LatAm, India, Mexico** (Long-distance **carpooling**, not on-demand city rides).
*   **Via:** **NYC, Chicago, DC, London, Berlin, etc.** (Shared rides / Shuttle-style, fixed routes).

---

### ⚠️ Critical Tips for Travelers
1.  **Download BEFORE you arrive:** Some apps require SMS verification (local SIM) or have app store region locks.
2.  **Payment Methods:** In many countries (SE Asia, LatAm, Africa), **Cash is King**. Ensure the app supports "Cash" payment if you don't have a local card/e-wallet (GrabPay, GoPay, Mercado Pago, M-Pesa).
3.  **Airport Pickups:** Airports often have strict geofences. The app pin might drop you at a "Kiss & Fly" zone, but the driver waits at a specific "Ride-Hailing Lot." **Always message the driver immediately after matching.**
4.  **Motorcycle Taxis:** In heavy traffic cities (Bangkok, Jakarta, Manila, São Paulo, Mexico City, Lagos, Nairobi), apps like **GrabBike, Gojek, Maxim, inDrive, Rapido, Angkas** offer 2-wheel rides—much faster/cheaper, but higher risk.
5.  **Safety:** Use "Share Trip" features. Verify **License Plate + Driver Photo + Name** before entering.

---

**Reply with your destination (City, Country) and I will tell you exactly which 1–2 apps to download and any local quirks to know.**

runs.u: Can you recommend a news outlet?
runs.reply:
There is no single "best" news outlet, as the right choice depends on **what you are looking for** (breaking news, deep analysis, specific beats, geographic focus) and **your tolerance for editorial perspective**.

Most media literacy experts recommend **consuming a "media diet" from multiple sources** across the political and institutional spectrum. Here is a breakdown of highly regarded outlets by category, along with context on their ownership and general reputation.

---

### 1. The "Wire Services" (The Primary Sources)
These are the backbone of global journalism. They sell feeds to other newspapers, TV stations, and websites. They prioritize speed, verification, and neutrality.
*   **Associated Press (AP):** US-based non-profit cooperative owned by its contributing newspapers. Widely considered the gold standard for straight, fact-based breaking news.
*   **Reuters:** Canadian-owned (Thomson Reuters). Similar reputation to AP; extremely strong on international finance, law, and global affairs.
*   **Agence France-Presse (AFP):** French state-owned but editorially independent. Excellent coverage of Africa, the Middle East, and Europe.

> **Best for:** Raw facts, breaking news alerts, avoiding editorial spin.

---

### 2. Major US National Newspapers (Deep Reporting & Investigative)
These have large newsrooms, rigorous editing standards, and distinct editorial pages (Opinion) separate from their News rooms.
*   **The New York Times:** Massive global footprint; strongest in US politics, international affairs, culture, and tech. *Perceived lean: Center-Left.*
*   **The Washington Post:** Exceptional on US federal government, national security, and politics. *Perceived lean: Center-Left.*
*   **The Wall Street Journal:** The gold standard for business, finance, and economics. News pages are widely respected as straight/center-right; Editorial page is distinctly conservative. *Perceived lean: Center (News) / Right (Opinion).*
*   **Los Angeles Times:** Strong on West Coast issues, entertainment, immigration, and Asia-Pacific. *Perceived lean: Center-Left.*

---

### 3. Major International Outlets (Global Perspective)
Essential for understanding how the US is viewed abroad and for coverage of regions US outlets often under-resource.
*   **The BBC (UK):** Publicly funded (license fee). Mandate for impartiality. Massive global bureau network. *Perceived lean: Center (UK context).*
*   **The Guardian (UK):** Owned by a trust (Scott Trust), no proprietor. Strong on climate, inequality, tech, and UK/EU politics. *Perceived lean: Left/Progressive.*
*   **The Economist (UK):** Weekly magazine/newspaper. Explicitly pro-free trade, pro-globalization, socially liberal. Famous for "leader" (unsigned editorial) articles. *Perceived lean: Center-Right (Classical Liberal).*
*   **Financial Times (UK/Japan-owned):** Premier global business paper; essential for finance, geopolitics, and energy transition. *Perceived lean: Center.*
*   **Al Jazeera English (Qatar-funded):** Unmatched access in the Global South, Middle East, and conflict zones. Editorial independence generally respected, though funding source is noted. *Perceived lean: Center-Left / Non-Western perspective.*
*   **Deutsche Welle (DW) / France 24 / NHK World:** State-funded international broadcasters (Germany, France, Japan) with strong English-language digital/video operations.

---

### 4. Non-Profit / Public Interest Journalism
Funded by donations/grants, no paywalls (usually), specific missions.
*   **ProPublica:** Pulitzer-winning investigative journalism. Focus: accountability, systems failure.
*   **NPR (National Public Radio) / PBS NewsHour:** US public media. Strong on audio/video storytelling, arts, culture, and nuanced policy coverage.
*   **The Texas Tribune / CalMatters / Chalkbeat:** Models for **state/local non-profit news**. If you want to know what is actually happening in your state legislature or school board, find your local non-profit newsroom.
*   **The Marshall Project:** Criminal justice focus.
*   **Grist / Inside Climate News:** Climate/environment focus.

---

### 5. Newsletters & "Explainer" Verticals (Curated Intelligence)
Good for cutting through noise.
*   **Axios / Semafor / The Bulwark / Tangle:** "Smart brevity" style. Axios/Semafor are generally centrist; The Bulwark is anti-Trump conservative; Tangle explicitly summarizes best arguments from Left and Right on one topic.
*   **Vox / The New York Times "The Morning" / Washington Post "The 7":** Explainer journalism.

---

### How to Evaluate a Source Yourself
When you land on a new site, check these three things immediately:

1.  **Ownership & Funding:** Who pays the bills? (Subscriptions? Ads? A billionaire? A government? A non-profit trust?) *Transparency here is a green flag.*
2.  **Corrections Policy:** Do they have a visible, accessible corrections page? Do they append corrections to the top of articles? *Professional newsrooms fix errors publicly.*
3.  **Separation of News vs. Opinion:** Is it labeled clearly? Reputable outlets wall off their reporters from their editorial board.

### Tools to Check Bias / Reliability
*   **AllSides / Ground News:** Show you how Left/Center/Right outlets are covering the *same story* simultaneously.
*   **Media Bias/Fact Check (MBFC):** Detailed breakdowns of funding, ownership, and factual reporting history.
*   **Ad Fontes Media (Interactive Media Bias Chart):** Rates outlets on a 2-axis graph: **Political Bias (L/R)** vs. **Reliability (Fact Reporting / Analysis / Opinion / Propaganda).**

---

### A "Starter Pack" Recommendation
If you want a balanced daily diet with minimal cost:
1.  **Wire Service Feed:** **AP News** or **Reuters** app (Free, no paywall, just facts).
2.  **One Major National Paper:** Subscribe to **NYT**, **WaPo**, or **WSJ** (paywalls support the reporting).
3.  **One International View:** **BBC World** or **Al Jazeera English** (Free apps/sites).
4.  **One Non-Profit/Local:** **Your local NPR station** + **ProPublica** (or your state non-profit like *The Texas Tribune*).
5.  **One "Cross-Cut" Tool:** **Ground News** or **Tangle Newsletter** to see blind spots.

---

*These organizations sell reporting to other news outlets. They prioritize speed, accuracy, and neutrality. They are the least "opinionated" sources available.*

*   **Associated Press (AP)** – US-based, nonprofit cooperative. Gold standard for straight reporting.
*   **Reuters** – UK-based, global reach. Similar reputation to AP for neutral, fact-based breaking news.
*   **Agence France-Presse (AFP)** – French-based, strong international coverage, especially Africa and Europe.

---

### 2. Major National Newspapers (Deep Reporting & Investigations)
*These have large newsrooms, high editorial standards, and distinct **editorial pages** (opinion) separate from their **newsrooms** (reporting).*

| Outlet | General Reputation | Note on Perspective |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **The New York Times** | Massive resources; best-in-class international & investigative reporting. | Newsroom: Center-Left. Editorial Page: Left. |
| **The Washington Post** | Strong on US politics, national security, tech. | Newsroom: Center-Left. Editorial Page: Left. |
| **The Wall Street Journal** | Gold standard for business, finance, economics. | Newsroom: Center/Center-Right. Editorial Page: Conservative. |
| **Los Angeles Times** | Strong on West Coast, immigration, entertainment, environment. | Newsroom: Center-Left. |
| **The Boston Globe** | Strong investigative team (Spotlight), New England focus. | Newsroom: Center-Left. |

---

### 3. Non-Profit / Public Media (Mission-Driven, No Paywalls Often)
*Funded by donations/grants, not ads or owners. Often focus on explanatory journalism.*

*   **NPR (National Public Radio)** – Audio-first. Strong national & cultural coverage. (Perceived Center-Left).
*   **PBS NewsHour** – TV/Video. Long-form interviews, very measured tone. (Perceived Center).
*   **ProPublica** – Pure investigative journalism. Partners with local papers. Pulitzer powerhouse.
*   **The Texas Tribune** / **CalMatters** / **Chalkbeat** – *Models for non-profit state/local news.* Check if your state has one.
*   **The Guardian (UK)** – Owned by a trust (non-profit structure). Strong global/environmental coverage. Explicitly progressive perspective.

---

### 4. International / Global Perspectives
*Essential if you want to see how the world views the US, or cover regions US media ignores.*

*   **BBC (UK)** – Vast global bureau network. Mandate for impartiality (sometimes criticized from all sides).
*   **Al Jazeera English (Qatar)** – Excellent Global South / Middle East / Africa coverage. Distinct from Al Jazeera Arabic.
*   **Deutsche Welle / DW (Germany)** – Strong Europe/Africa focus, fact-checking focus.
*   **France 24** – Strong Francophone Africa & Europe coverage.
*   **The Economist (UK)** – Weekly magazine. Center-right economically, socially liberal. *Analysis/Opinion heavy, not breaking news.*

---

### 5. Specialized / Niche (Best for Specific Topics)
*   **Tech:** *The Verge, Ars Technica, TechCrunch, 404 Media (worker-owned).*
*   **Science/Health:** *Stat News, Nature, Science Magazine, Undark.*
*   **Legal/SCOTUS:** *SCOTUSblog (gold standard), Lawfare.*
*   **Foreign Policy:** *Foreign Affairs, Foreign Policy, War on the Rocks.*
*   **Fact-Checking:** *Snopes, PolitiFact, FactCheck.org, Lead Stories.*

---

### 6. Tools to Help You Navigate Bias & Reliability
Instead of trusting a label, use these methodologies to evaluate specific articles:

1.  **AllSides / Ground News** – Show the same story covered by Left, Center, and Right outlets side-by-side.
2.  **Ad Fontes Media (Media Bias Chart)** – Rates outlets on **Reliability (Fact vs. Opinion)** and **Bias (Left vs. Right)**.
3.  **Media Bias/Fact Check (MBFC)** – Searchable database with detailed methodology for specific URLs.

---

### A Practical "Starter Pack" Recommendation
If you want a balanced, low-effort daily routine:

1.  **Morning Briefing:** **AP News** or **Reuters** app (Free, neutral, just the facts).
2.  **Deep Dive (Pick One):** **NYT** or **WaPo** (for politics/institutions) **OR** **WSJ** (for business/economy).
3.  **Long-form/Weekend:** **The Economist** (global view) or **The Atlantic / New Yorker** (essays/culture).
4.  **Local:** **Subscribe to your local non-profit paper** (e.g., *The Baltimore Banner, The Minnesota Reformer, Spotlight PA*). *Local accountability journalism is the most endangered and most impactful.*
5.  **Check the Other Side:** Once a week, scan **Ground News** or **AllSides** on a major story to see what the "other side" is emphasizing or ignoring.

---

### ⚠️ Red Flags to Avoid
*   **Outlets that don't correct errors prominently.**
*   **Sites where "News" and "Opinion" are visually indistinguishable.**
*   **Outlets funded by a single billionaire, political party, or government without editorial independence firewalls.**
*   **Headlines written purely for rage-bait/clicks (e.g., "DESTROYS," "SLAMS," "ERUPTS").**

**What are you trying to achieve?** (e.g., "I want to understand the economy," "I want to know what my representative is doing," "I want to avoid US-centric news") — I can give a much more specific list if you tell me your goal.
